transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-05-19
Start time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Alicia Gomez (HelixBio - Head of ML Ops), Mohammed Khan (HelixBio - Infra Lead), Sofia Duarte (HelixBio - Security)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough):
- Focus: on-prem / air-gapped delivery of Redwood runtime artifacts, offline licensing, GPU driver validation, and baseline performance expectations (latency/throughput).
- Agreed next steps: SE to send packaging checklist & signed tar format; customer to share traffic profile; plan 2-day onsite pilot for driver validation.

Topics:
- artifact packaging and integrity (tarball, GPG, sha256)
- offline license activation and verification model
- GPU driver matrix (CUDA/NVIDIA vs ROCm), container runtimes in air-gapped env
- runtime tuning: KV cache warmup, batching, quantization tradeoffs for p95/p99
- rollout & rollback in isolated networks

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: ok hi everyone thanks for joining, I know we have a tight schedule so we'll try to keep it focused. i'm jordan from redwood, AE, and with me is priya, our SE.
[00:21] Priya Nair: hey all, hi, nice to meet you, i'll be the technical lead on the packaging and install side. if anyone's on a different timezone let us know.
[00:34] Alicia Gomez: thanks, appreciate it. we wanted to do a deep dive because our security team requires an air-gapped install and we need to understand artifact and license flows plus perf.
[00:47] Mohammed Khan: yes, and we run everything in our locked lab, no internet egress from the inference nodes, so driver install and certs are manual.
[01:02] Sofia Duarte: from security, main concerns are tamper-proof artifacts, chain of custody, and offline license verification that does not phone home.
[01:16] Jordan Lee: totally, that aligns with our offline model. priya — quick outline?
[01:24] Priya Nair: sure. i'll walk through the artifact bundle, verification steps (sha256 + GPG), driver matrix and a few install gotchas, then we'll go into runtime knobs — batching, kv-cache, quantize settings and baseline numbers we typically see.
[01:38] Priya Nair: note: some transcription of product names might be off in the recording — you'll see k-v cash spelled weird sometimes.
[01:46] Alicia Gomez: (laughs) we've seen that in other transcripts. ok please go ahead.

[03:10] Priya Nair: Artifact bundle: for air-gapped installs we provide a signed tarball that contains: container images as OCI tar (or our flattened filesystem), a verified install script, a platform compatibility matrix, and the offline license file template. The tar is accompanied by a .sha256 and a GPG detached signature.
[03:32] Priya Nair: Customer can verify using gpg --verify and sha256sum -c locally. we can also provide a java/py small verifier if you want.
[03:45] Mohammed Khan: what about the container runtime? we use containerd with cri and don't want to use docker.sock, any problems?
[03:55] Priya Nair: containerd is supported — we produce OCI images and also an option for a rootfs tar that you can run with runc/containerd. if your infra requires a specific snapshotter, tell us and we can produce images compatible with it.
[04:09] Sofia Duarte: do you sign images with cosign or gpg? our pipeline uses cosign attestation.
[04:18] Priya Nair: we currently sign the tar with GPG and include sha256 sums; we are piloting cosign-based attestations — we can adapt to cosign for enterprise customers.

[05:30] Priya Nair: Licensing: offline license is a signed license file tied to a hardware/fingerprint or to a cluster id. we avoid phone-home — validation is local cryptographic check of signature and expiry. if you need HSM-backed activation, we can provide an offline activation token flow where you copy a challenge file to a networked admin machine, sign it via our portal, then bring back a signed token.
[05:52] Alicia Gomez: challenge/response sounds ok, but timeline wise would that fit our procurement? we prefer a single-file license if possible.
[06:03] Jordan Lee: we can do both — default is a single signed license file (PKI signed by Redwood). challenge/response is for HSM-required customers. we'll include diagrams in the doc.

[07:20] Mohammed Khan: for the license file validation, what's embedded? machine id, cluster name, CPU or GPU fingerprint? we need to know how brittle it is for live upgrades.
[07:33] Priya Nair: typical fields: customer id, allowed model list, node count or vCPU/GPU entitlements, expiry. we prefer cluster-level ids (a UUID you generate) rather than hardware serial numbers, because nodes often get replaced. rolling upgrades won't break the license as long as the cluster id stays the same.
[07:54] Sofia Duarte: and audit logs? we need local audit of license validation events.
[08:01] Priya Nair: the runtime writes an audit entry to syslog/journalctl and to the local Red audit file under /var/log/redwood/license-audit.log. we can ship with a facility to forward logs to your SIEM if you want.

[09:15] Priya Nair: Drivers and GPU matrix: please confirm your GPU models, drivers and CUDA/ROCm matrix. we support NVIDIA with CUDA 11.8+ and CUDA 12.x, recommended NVIDIA driver 535+ for A100/A40 families; for AMD (ROCm) we have an experimental path but it's not fully validated for the biggest models.
[09:41] Mohammed Khan: we have 4x A40s per node, currently on driver 520.xx and CUDA 11.7. would that be a blocker?
[09:50] Priya Nair: 520 is older — you'll want to upgrade to 535+ for the best kernels; 11.7 may miss some perf improvements. we can run a compatibility shim but recommend driver upgrade during the pilot.
[10:06] Alicia Gomez: upgrade risk is our main ops story — can the install be done offline? drivers too?
[10:15] Priya Nair: yes, drivers can be supplied as signed driver bundles in the tar. our install script has a driver-verify step that checks the exact kernel module and nvidia-smi output. we also include prebuilt cuDNN and NCCL libs where possible.

[11:40] Priya Nair: Now runtime knobs. first: KV cache. we do a prefix KV cache which is persisted per model; warmup matters — a cold cache p95 can be 2–3x higher than warm. we recommend prewarmed caches for steady-state low-latency apps.
[12:05] Mohammed Khan: how do we prewarm in an air-gapped env, do you provide a script?
[12:12] Priya Nair: yes we provide a cache-warm utility: feed in a representative set of prompts or run a replay of traces and it will populate the KV stores. it's in the bundle. you'll need to ensure KV path is on fast NVMe.
[12:25] Alicia Gomez: ok NVMe is fine. what's the per-token latency hit for KV fetches?
[12:32] Priya Nair: on A40 with optimized kernels and warm cache we see p50 ~8–12ms per token for medium sequences (512 tokens) in streaming mode; p95 varies with batching and concurrency — we commonly quote p95 ~60–120ms depending on batch size and sequence length.
[12:52] Alicia Gomez: that's a big range, can you give an example with numbers for batch sizes?
[13:02] Priya Nair: sure — example: single-request (no batching) with seq512, p95 ~90ms. With micro-batching (batch size 4) throughput increases but p95 could jump to ~150ms if you wait to fill batch; with continuous batching (async fill) and a max-latency window of 20ms we can keep p95 closer to 100ms and increase tokens/sec by ~2.5x.

[14:40] Mohammed Khan: quantization — we were considering int8 to save memory, any caveats?
[14:47] Priya Nair: quantize helps throughput and memory; int8 gives 2–4x memory reductions and often ~1.8x perf improvement for decoder-only models. but quality regressions vary. we recommend per-model evals on your prompt set. also we do group-quantization and KV cache format adjustments; sometimes kv cache needs a different packing for int8 to keep perf.
[15:12] Alicia Gomez: do you ship quantized model artifacts as separate files in the bundle?
[15:18] Priya Nair: yes, we can include FP16 and INT8 variants and a manifest that indicates supported runtime flags. the offline license can also constrain which model variants are allowed.

[16:45] Jordan Lee: there's usually an ask about deterministic kernels and kernel selection when people upgrade drivers — how brittle is perf?
[16:55] Priya Nair: kernel selection is done at startup by our runtime — it probes for available kernels and picks the best-fit. upgrades can change the chosen kernel and therefore perf. for stable perf we recommend pinning the runtime config to a kernel family and keeping the driver within validated range. we'll provide a recommended driver/kernel matrix in the compatibility doc.

[18:03] Mohammed Khan: about NVLink and inter-GPU comms — we don't use NVSwitch, just NVLink between pairs. any NCCL considerations?
[18:12] Priya Nair: we use NCCL for multi-gpu; network and p2p topology affect throughput. in your topology we can tune NCCL to prefer P2P where available and fallback to PCIe paths. we include a small perf harness to map bandwidth and choose the right NCCL config.

[19:30] Alicia Gomez: security — how to ensure artifacts haven't been tampered with during transport to our air-gapped facility?
[19:38] Priya Nair: GPG detached signature + sha256 plus an optional cosign attestation. we recommend verifying signatures on the import machine before moving artifacts to the secure network. maintain chain-of-custody logs — we provide a checklist.

[21:00] Sofia Duarte: for compliance, we need a reproducible build id for artifacts and to be able to verify we received the exact build we tested. does your release manifest include build metadata?
[21:10] Priya Nair: yes every tar includes a manifest.json with build id, git sha, model hash, and kernel version used to compile. we also include the exact conda/pip list if the user wants to inspect.

[22:30] Mohammed Khan: ok can you walk us through a sample offline install sequence?
[22:36] Priya Nair: example: 1) transfer tarball to bastion outside air-gapped network, 2) verify gpg signature and sha256, 3) extract to staging, 4) run ./redwood-install --verify-drivers to check current driver and kernel, 5) optionally run ./redwood-install --apply-drivers to install from the bundle, 6) apply license with ./redwood-license apply --file license.redwood, 7) start runtime and run the perf-harness to validate. we'll include an idempotent mode so retries are safe.
[23:12] Alicia Gomez: does license.apply require root? we have least-privilege rules.
[23:18] Priya Nair: license apply requires an admin user but not root; we do a file-level check and place the license under /etc/redwood/license; the runtime reads it as a non-root service.

[24:40] Jordan Lee: let's talk about metrics and observability in air-gapped mode. you still want per-token cost breakdowns?
[24:48] Priya Nair: yes, we emit local telemetry to a file. for air-gapped customers we can provide an encrypted telemetry bundle that you can ship out-of-band for support, or you can forward to your internal Prometheus stack. we do not require sending telemetry to Redwood unless you opt in.

[26:10] Mohammed Khan: what about rollout strategies — can we do canary on-prem?
[26:16] Priya Nair: yes, runtime supports canary and A/B rollouts by model tag. in air-gapped mode you can stage multiple model directories and map traffic rules to them. rollback is file-swap + service restart. we recommend blue/green for major updates.

[28:05] Alicia Gomez: performance baseline — can you give concrete tokens/sec numbers for our target model (we plan to use a Llama-2-70B-like backbone)?
[28:15] Priya Nair: for Llama-2-70B equivalent on 4x A40, in FP16 we typically see ~120–180 tokens/sec depending on sequence length and KV locality. INT8 can push that to ~200–300 tokens/sec but depends on optimized kernels and driver. these are ballpark numbers; we need to run benchmarks with your exact prompt shapes.
[28:42] Mohammed Khan: our tokens are usually 256 average with spikes to 1024 occasionally. will spikes cause long tail latencies?
[28:52] Priya Nair: yes spikes increase p95/p99. we recommend configuring an admission controller that allows short bursts but enforces a max tokens-per-second per key. also prefix caching reduces tail when many requests share prefixes.

[30:10] Priya Nair: batching policy suggestions: use adaptive batching with a latency cap (e.g., 20ms) to balance throughput/latency. for interactive workloads, keep batch sizes small (2–8). for high-throughput offline requests, batch larger and run async.

[31:25] Jordan Lee: question from procurement perspective — is the offline license perpetual or time-bound?
[31:33] Alicia Gomez: (interjects) we prefer term licenses but can do annual renewals.
[31:38] Jordan Lee: typically we do term-based licenses with offline activation; perpetual options available for large-enterprise. we'll include pricing notes.

[33:00] Mohammed Khan: during the driver upgrade, can we preserve existing runtime config and cache?
[33:06] Priya Nair: runtime config is preserved; KV cache format is compatible across minor driver updates but a major quantize change might require cache rebuild. we will warn if cache needs migration and provide a migration tool.

[34:40] Sofia Duarte: for audits we need to capture the exact license validation events — is the audit file signed?
[34:46] Priya Nair: audit entries can be exported and signed by your internal key; we can also ship a small tool to sign the export for your chain-of-custody.

[36:10] Priya Nair: gotcha — now a short demo of the perf-harness (high level): it runs replay traces, supports config for batch size, max-latency window, concurrency, and outputs p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec plus GPU utilization. the harness can be run in isolated mode and writes a results.json.
[36:37] Alicia Gomez: will the harness include scripts to generate the warmup traces from our logs?
[36:42] Priya Nair: yes, we can provide a small parser to convert your logs to the harness format.

[38:05] Mohammed Khan: any gotchas for kernel modules, like nvidia-uvm conflicts? we've hit issues before.
[38:12] Priya Nair: yep, nvidia-uvm needs to be loaded; we check for common conflicting modules in the verify-drivers step. if you have secure-boot on, modules may need signing; we document that flow.

[40:00] Jordan Lee: let's go into a few troubleshooting scenarios quickly. if p95 increases after driver upgrade: what do we look at?
[40:08] Priya Nair: check chosen kernels, GPU clock rates, NCCL fallback paths, and whether the runtime selected a slower attention kernel. we include an option to force a kernel family, and a diagnostic that captures per-layer time breakdown.

[42:12] Sofia Duarte: data residency — logs written by runtime, any PII leak risk?
[42:19] Priya Nair: no PII is sent anywhere; logs are local. content data is not included in telemetry by default; if you opt in we hash identifiers and keep content out. we can sign an attestation.

[44:00] Alicia Gomez: ok, happy with the plan — let's summarize next steps.
[44:06] Jordan Lee: recap: Priya will send packaging checklist and signed sample tar; Alicia will send token histograms and traces; Mohammed confirms driver baseline; Jordan will send license flow and procurement notes. We'll schedule pilot week for driver validation.
[44:23] Priya Nair: action items and due dates are recorded in the follow-up email i'll send.
[44:30] Mohammed Khan: two quick Qs — can you include a script to compute sha256 of a whole folder recursively? and can we get an example license file?
[44:40] Priya Nair: yes to both — included in the bundle.

[46:00] (brief silence and off-topic chat about lunch)

[48:10] Alicia Gomez: one last thing from security: SAML/sso for console and role-based access in air-gapped mode — any limitations?
[48:19] Priya Nair: for the console we support SAML SSO via an on-prem identity provider; in fully air-gapped installs an internal IdP is required. RBAC is enforced locally and maps to SAML groups; we will provide mapping examples.

[50:05] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts. any objections to the pilot week timeframe?
[50:12] Mohammed Khan: week of 6/9 works.
[50:16] Alicia Gomez: yes fine.
[50:20] Sofia Duarte: ok great, thanks.

[51:00] End of meeting.

Notes about transcription quality: speaker labels are mostly correct but some technical terms transcribed imperfectly (e.g., k-v "cash" instead of cache), and some timestamps are approximate.
